item.title: 50% and Rising: Why Trump's Tariffs on India Are Colliding With the Russian Oil Trade
item.body:
## A Trade Relationship Under Strain

The United States and India have spent two decades building what both governments once called a "natural partnership." That relationship is now being tested by one of the steepest tariff regimes Washington has placed on any major trading partner. Combined U.S. tariffs on Indian goods have climbed to roughly 50%, a level that puts India in the same bracket as countries facing the harshest U.S. trade penalties. At the center of the dispute is a commodity India does not produce in meaningful quantities at home: crude oil.

## How the Tariffs Stacked Up

The increase did not happen all at once. Earlier in 2025, the Trump administration imposed a baseline tariff on Indian imports as part of a broader push to rebalance U.S. trade relationships with countries running persistent surpluses with the United States. That baseline was later doubled with an additional tariff explicitly tied to India's continued purchases of Russian crude oil, which U.S. officials argue helps fund Russia's war effort in Ukraine despite Western sanctions.

Indian officials have pushed back, noting that the United States and European Union continued trading with Russia in other sectors even as they criticized New Delhi, and that India's energy purchases have been conducted through legal channels rather than sanctioned entities. New Delhi has also pointed out that Russian oil imports were, in earlier years, tacitly welcomed by Western governments as a way to keep global energy markets stable and prevent price spikes after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

## Why Indian Refiners Kept Buying

For India's refining industry, the economics have been difficult to ignore. Russian crude has traded at a meaningful discount to global benchmark prices since Western buyers largely stepped back from the market. Indian refiners, both state-owned and private, expanded their purchases sharply after 2022, turning Russia into one of India's top crude suppliers within a few years.

Industry data reviewed by market analysts indicates that Indian imports of Russian crude remained elevated through August 2025, even as the tariff threat intensified. Refiners have cited existing supply contracts, logistics already in motion, and the absence of comparably priced alternatives as reasons purchases did not stop immediately. Some Indian refiners have reportedly begun diversifying supply sources in response to pressure, but analysts caution that a full pivot away from discounted Russian barrels would take time and could raise fuel costs for Indian consumers and businesses.

## The Economic Stakes for India

India is one of the world's largest crude oil importers, relying on foreign suppliers for the large majority of its energy needs. Government officials have framed continued access to affordable crude as a matter of economic and energy security for a country still developing its infrastructure and lifting large populations out of poverty. A sudden shift away from discounted supply, officials argue, would raise costs across the economy, from transportation to manufacturing to household energy bills.

At the same time, the U.S. tariffs threaten sectors of the Indian economy that have little to do with energy, including textiles, gems and jewelry, and pharmaceuticals, industries that employ large numbers of workers and depend heavily on U.S. demand. Indian exporters in these sectors have warned that sustained tariffs at current levels could cost jobs and shrink order books, even as trade negotiators from both countries continue periodic talks aimed at finding a resolution.

## Diplomatic Signals and What Comes Next

Despite the tariff dispute, both governments have generally avoided framing the disagreement as a broader rupture in the U.S.-India relationship, which also includes cooperation on defense, technology, and regional security matters. Officials on both sides have signaled openness to further negotiations, and trade delegations have continued to meet periodically to discuss a path forward.

Analysts following the talks say a resolution will likely hinge on some combination of India adjusting its energy sourcing, the United States offering carve-outs or phased reductions, and progress on other elements of a long-discussed bilateral trade agreement. Until an agreement is reached, however, the 50% tariff wall remains in place, and Indian refiners face a genuine trade-off between near-term cost savings on Russian crude and the broader economic cost of strained trade relations with one of India's largest export markets.

For now, neither side has signaled an immediate willingness to fully back down, leaving businesses on both sides of the Pacific watching closely for the next round of talks.
